title: Scientists Map the Orbit of Two Flaring Dwarf Stars 59 Light-Years Away! 🔭
body: Scientists Map the Orbit of Two Flaring Dwarf Stars 59 Light-Years Away! 🔭
A team of scientists has successfully mapped the orbit of a binary star system called DG CVn, made up of two red dwarf stars — small, dim stars — orbiting each other.

What is exciting is that the two stars emit radio waves, so scientists observed them with a network of 10 radio telescopes spread across North America working together as a single giant telescope, over a span of 18 years.
This method could help in the future to discover hidden planets orbiting active stars that are hard to detect with ordinary methods. An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star outside our Solar System.

The system is about 59.3 light-years away, its orbit lasts 4.511 years and is highly elliptical, with a closest approach of 0.59 astronomical units — less than the distance between the Earth and the Sun.
